Coverage is reasonably broad, spanning super-resolution, deraining, denoising, JPEG artifact removal, multiple backbones, qualitative examples, and reduced-precision inference. Some improvements are substantial, such as +0.62 dB on Urban100 and +0.81 dB on Manga109 for HAT ×4 super-resolution.
The manuscript is generally readable and the figures communicate the reported activation behavior effectively.
weaknesses: The principal normalization component, LN*, is mathematically equivalent to GroupNorm with one group: both normalize each sample over all spatial and channel dimensions and then apply channel-wise affine parameters. GroupNorm is neither cited nor evaluated. Moreover, Table 3 indicates that most of the improvement already comes from this known operation, while the proposed rescaling adds only about 0.017–0.086 dB in the sole reported ablation. This substantially weakens the novelty claim.

The causal account is not established. LayerNorm's statistics are input-dependent, contrary to the paper's repeated characterization of it as input-independent, and per-token normalization does not by itself prove that spatial correlations are disrupted. The RPE and bias visualizations are qualitative, with no controlled intervention or quantitative correlation analysis demonstrating that networks deliberately amplify channels to bypass LayerNorm.

The central diagnostics are insufficiently defined. The manuscript does not provide reproducible formulas and aggregation details for its feature-scale and channel-entropy measurements, nor variation across images, batches, seeds, or training runs. Large but finite residual-stream activations are called divergence even though the models converge, leaving the relationship to optimization stability unclear.

The evaluation lacks statistical rigor. Results appear to be single runs without uncertainty estimates. Several denoising and JPEG gains are very small and could plausibly reflect run-to-run variation; the claimed consistent improvement is also contradicted by cases such as SwinIR at JPEG quality 10, where LIVE1 PSNR decreases and Classic5 is unchanged.

Comparisons use simplified, self-reimplemented 300K-iteration training rather than published checkpoints or competitive state-of-the-art training recipes. Exact architecture configurations, parameter counts, computational cost, and the capacity and schedule denoted by HAT† are not reported. Consequently, it is unclear whether the method improves converged competitive models or mainly changes optimization speed/effective scaling in an undertrained regime.

Global spatial-channel normalization makes predictions depend on image extent and tiling. This is especially concerning because training uses small crops and some Urban100 evaluations use nonstandard 256×256 sub-patches. The paper does not test full-image versus tiled inference, changing test resolution, or other distribution shifts needed to support the claimed drop-in applicability.

The reduced-precision study is too underspecified to support deployment claims: quantization granularity, calibration, clipping, and implementation are omitted, and the catastrophic all-FP16 baseline is not compared with standard mixed-precision practice, FP32 normalization/reductions, BF16, or activation-aware quantization. No latency, memory, or hardware-efficiency measurements are reported.

Reproducibility is inadequate overall: there is no code or resource statement, several model and measurement details are missing, and the nonstandard evaluation protocol is not specified sufficiently for independent replication. These novelty, evidence, and reproducibility issues make the submission uncompetitive for a top-tier venue despite its interesting empirical observations.

Most main-table results are single runs, including many improvements of only 0.01–0.10 dB, with no confidence intervals or significance analysis. Gains become quite small for the full-size HAT setting. Stronger comparisons against established restoration-specific normalization variants and competitive complete systems are also missing.

The claimed real-world evaluation uses synthetically degraded training and test images rather than real captured degradations. The quantization study omits essential details such as calibration, granularity, scaling, accumulation precision, and runtime, while naive all-FP16 execution is not representative of standard mixed-precision deployment.

Global image-dependent statistics may make results sensitive to test resolution, padding, crops, and tiled inference, all important in restoration deployment, but none of these behaviors is evaluated.

Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of released code and multiple internal inconsistencies: HAT2 is described as trained for both 300K and 500K iterations, Table 6 reports a likely erroneous Set14 SSIM of .8276, and several figure/table references point to unrelated material. These issues make the otherwise detailed appendix difficult to trust.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and practically relevant feature-magnitude pathology in image-restoration Transformers and studies it across model scales and restoration tasks.

The proposed i-LN is simple and is evaluated across multiple backbones, super-resolution scales, and four restoration tasks, with especially notable gains for lightweight super-resolution and deraining models.
The component ablations support complementary benefits from spatially holistic normalization and input-adaptive residual scaling.
The low-precision experiments and multi-seed real-world degradation study provide useful evidence beyond standard benchmark accuracy.
The appendix supplies extensive qualitative results and many architecture and training details.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification does not establish the central causal claims. Proposition 2 analyzes normalization before the affine transformation, whereas the implemented channel-wise affine scale generally destroys the claimed homothety. Moreover, neither proposition covers the attention/FFN transformation or residual block, and latent-token distances are not clearly equivalent to image spatial correlations.

The proof of Proposition 1 informally compares coefficients that themselves determine token-dependent means and variances; under the paper's finite-token definition, the asserted characterization of the exceptional cases is not adequately justified.

The channel-entropy measure applies softmax directly to unnormalized activation magnitudes. It is inherently scale-sensitive, so magnitude growth alone can cause apparent entropy collapse; this does not independently demonstrate increasing channel imbalance.

Novelty is insufficiently positioned against closely related global LayerNorm, GroupNorm, and other spatial/channel normalization or adaptive-scaling methods. The novelty of the specific combination, rather than its application to restoration, remains unclear.

Most main results use reduced-capacity models and apparently single runs. Under the official full HAT configuration, gains shrink to roughly 0–0.15 dB, the baseline is copied from prior work rather than retrained, and uncertainty or significance is not reported. Denoising and JPEG gains are frequently very small.

Claims based on visually structured relative-position embeddings are subjective and lack a quantitative spatial-correlation measure. The quantization protocol is also underspecified, and catastrophic pure-FP16 inference may not represent standard mixed-precision deployment.
Practical consequences of global spatial statistics—runtime, memory, image-size dependence, and tiled-inference inconsistency—are not evaluated despite the drop-in and deployment claims.

Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of code and several inconsistencies or omissions: HAT2 is described as both 300K and 500K iterations, Table 6 contains an implausible Set14 SSIM value, real-world results are cross-referenced incorrectly, and details such as normalization epsilon, evaluation preprocessing, quantization, gradient clipping, and KL regularization are missing.
